title: The magicians
hookLine: Pharaoh's magicians throw their ropes, Musa's staff swallows them, and they fall down believing

lines: A CONTEST ON A FESTIVAL DAY.
cards: Who can tell a real diamond from a fake? A jeweler. A forged painting from the real one?
The expert who has spent a lifetime with the brush. The people hardest to fool are the ones who know every trick. Pharaoh has heard Musa out, seen the staff and the hand, and calls it sorcery.
So he sets up a contest: a festival day, the people gathered in the morning light. He summons every skilled magician in the land, and they come to win. They even ask about the reward.
Pharaoh says: yes, and you'll be among those close to me.

teach.b: Surah Ta-Ha sets the scene. The magicians say: Musa, will you throw first, or shall we? He says: you throw.
They throw down their ropes and staffs, and by their magic it seems to Musa that they're moving, writhing.
And the Qur'an tells us something honest: Musa felt a fear inside himself. Even a prophet, even after the valley. He's told: don't be afraid.
You are the one who will prevail. Throw what is in your right hand. Remember the question in the valley?
He throws the staff, and it swallows everything they made. Then the moment that turns the story.
The magicians fall down in prostration: we believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa. They didn't need a debate. They were the experts.
They knew exactly what a trick looked like from the inside, and this wasn't one.
They knew the real thing. Pharaoh is furious. You believed before I gave you permission?

He threatens the worst punishment he can think of: hands and feet cut off, crucifixion on palm trunks. And the men who came that morning asking about their reward answer him: decide whatever you'll decide.
You can only decide about this life of the world. In a single morning they go from Pharaoh's hired experts to people he can't frighten.
A saying in the commentaries puts it this way: they began the day as magicians and ended it as believers.

how: Muslims often tell the story of Pharaoh's magicians as an example of sudden, sincere faith, and of courage in the face of threats; it is recounted in several surahs of the Qur'an.

o: foreign sorcerers who came to help Musa
Pharaoh's priests who served his gods
experts in tricks who knew this was no trick

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: you believed before I allowed it?

s: the Qur'an says Musa felt no fear at the contest
it says he felt a fear inside himself, and was told: don't be afraid.
the magicians fell down in prostration and believed
they said: we believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa.
the magicians backed down when Pharaoh threatened them
they said: decide whatever you'll decide. you can only decide about this life.

games.q: you're one of Pharaoh's magicians. you've thrown your ropes, and Musa's staff has swallowed them all. you know every trick there is. what do you do?
o: insist it was a better trick than yours.
fall down in prostration: we believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa.
games.why: they fell down believing, in front of Pharaoh. the experts knew it wasn't a trick, and his threats couldn't move them.

practice: The magicians changed their minds in public, in front of the king, with everything to lose; you only have to do it privately.

Think of one opinion you held with confidence that turned out to be wrong, about a person, a place or yourself, and say it plainly: I was wrong about that. Notice how the chest feels, and if you pray, give thanks for being shown.

wordCard.voice: The magicians: Pharaoh's experts, who knew a trick when they saw one, and knew this wasn't.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 20:70: "in prostration" — the magicians fell down this way. same root as sajda and masjid.

carryVoice: Your line: they knew the real thing. It took experts to see it. Day fifty-two, done.
